modalities.name: Received, Then Given
modalities.tagline: Receive a wish from imagined ideal parents, then pass it on.
modalities.whatItIs: Received, Then Given is an untested concept that links the imagined caregivers of the Ideal Parent Figure Protocol with the goodwill phrases of loving-kindness meditation. First you imagine ideal parent figures offering you one simple wish, such as 'may you feel safe', and let yourself take it in; then you offer that same wish, in the same tone, to one real person in your life. The scenes are imagined rather than remembered: it uses only memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill can be hard to give when it was rarely received, and many people find kindness phrases hollow for that reason. Receiving a wish first, from imagined parents who mean it, and then handing exactly that wish on is meant to let care flow from something you have just felt rather than from effort alone.
modalities.whatYouDo: In four to six weekly sessions with a therapist trained in attachment-focused imagery, you settle with a short body scan, imagine ideal parent figures with you as a child and hear them offer one wish, staying with how it feels in the body for a few minutes. You then picture one real person, starting with someone easy such as a friend or a child you know, and silently offer them the same words, noticing whether the warmth carries over. At home you repeat the two steps for about 15 minutes a few times a week with a recording, keeping one wish for a week before trying another, and each session begins by reviewing what carried over and what felt hollow.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find loving-kindness phrases empty and suspect it is because kindness was scarce early on. It may also suit those who want attachment-focused imagery to reach outward into their real relationships.
modalities.cautions: This is an untested idea, and imagined care can stir grief about what was missing in your real childhood, so work with a therapist trained in both attachment imagery and trauma, keep home practice short and pause if old pain comes up strongly. It should not replace established treatment for depression, PTSD or other conditions, and anyone in crisis should seek professional help first.
modalities.tweet: Kindness can be hard to give when you rarely got it. Received, Then Given is an untested idea: imagine ideal parents offering you a wish like 'may you feel safe', take it in, then pass the same wish to one real person. Begun with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Resting on Their Care
modalities.tagline: Hold one felt quality of imagined care as your meditation object.
modalities.whatItIs: Resting on Their Care is a speculative concentration practice that borrows its object from the Ideal Parent Figure Protocol. Instead of the breath, you briefly imagine ideal parent figures showing one quality, such as protection or soothing, then let the picture fade and rest attention on the bodily feeling it leaves, returning to that feeling each time the mind wanders. Only memories you already have are involved, images and feelings are not treated as evidence of what happened, and nothing is used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: Concentration tends to settle more easily on a pleasant, steady object, and the felt sense of being cared for may be one. Holding a single quality of care steadily, rather than moving through a whole scene, is meant to let that feeling become calmer, longer lasting and more familiar.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist who also teaches meditation guides the first sessions: after a short body scan, you imagine ideal parents showing one quality for a minute or two, then drop the images and hold the warmth, steadiness or ease it leaves in the chest or belly as your single object for 10 to 20 minutes. When attention drifts or the feeling fades, you briefly call up the same quality and return to resting on it, keeping to one quality for a week or more before trying another. Between sessions you practice at home with a recording, and sits stay short until they feel stable.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who already do some attachment-focused imagery and want a quieter, steadier way to stay with it. It may also suit meditators who find the breath a dry or anxious object.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: imagined care can bring up grief about your real childhood, and absorbed concentration can sometimes bring fear, unusual body sensations or low mood afterward, so work with a therapist trained in attachment imagery and trauma who also knows meditation-related difficulties, keep sits short and do not take it onto an intensive retreat. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should be screened by a clinician before starting, and it is not a substitute for treatment.
modalities.tweet: A new concept for meditators: Resting on Their Care. You picture ideal parent figures protecting or soothing you, let the picture go, and hold the feeling it leaves as your point of focus. Kept short, and learned with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Matched in Motion
modalities.tagline: A dance therapist mirrors your movement while you imagine attuned parents.
modalities.whatItIs: Matched in Motion is a new, untested concept between the Ideal Parent Figure Protocol and dance movement therapy. Tuning in to a child's feelings is one of the five qualities of ideal parents, and much early tuning in happens without words, through a caregiver matching a baby's rhythm, energy and gestures; here a dance movement therapist mirrors your movements while you imagine ideal parent figures moving with you in the same attuned way. It works with what you feel now and with imagined figures, not with memories, and nothing in it is used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: Being accurately matched can make a person feel seen without anything being said. Feeling a real person follow your movement, and then imagining ideal parents doing the same, is meant to give imagined attunement a physical, felt reference point.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a small group of four to six, or one to one, a dance movement therapist trained in attachment work leads 60-minute weekly sessions that open with a gentle warm-up to soft music. You then move slowly however you like, swaying, reaching or rocking from foot to foot, while the therapist mirrors your rhythm and shape at a short distance without touching, and after a few minutes you close your eyes, keep moving and imagine ideal parent figures matching you in the same way. The session ends seated, with a few words about what it was like to be matched and which moments felt most tuned in.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find imagery work too abstract and feel things more readily through the body. It may suit those who rarely felt understood without having to explain themselves.
modalities.cautions: Untested: being closely watched and matched can feel exposing at first and may stir grief about your real childhood, so it belongs with a credentialed dance movement therapist with trauma training, and you can open your eyes, sit down or stop at any time. Use a clear, non-slip floor, warm up first, keep movements within your own range of joints and balance, stop if you feel dizzy, faint or unwell, and no touch is used.
modalities.tweet: Picture moving slowly to soft music while a dance therapist mirrors your every sway, then closing your eyes and imagining ideal parents doing the same. Matched in Motion is a speculative idea for feeling understood without words, guided by a trained therapist.

modalities.name: The Critic's Real Wish
modalities.tagline: Turn a critical part's hidden hope for you into a kind wish.
modalities.whatItIs: The Critic's Real Wish is a proposed practice that combines the parts work of Internal Family Systems with the goodwill phrases of loving-kindness meditation. Parts work assumes that even a harsh inner critic is trying to help, so you ask a familiar critical part what it is really hoping for you and turn the answer into a wish you then offer to yourself. You work only with parts you already know, nothing is used to dig up forgotten events, and whatever comes up is treated as inner experience rather than evidence about the past.
modalities.coreIdea: A critic that shouts 'don't embarrass yourself' may, underneath, want you to be safe and respected, and putting that hope into gentle words gives it a voice that does not hurt. Saying the wish on the critic's behalf is meant to honor the part's concern while dropping its harsh tone.
modalities.whatYouDo: In two or three sessions with a therapist trained in parts work, you find a critical part you know well, notice how you feel toward it, and ask what it fears would happen if it stopped criticizing and what it most wants for you. Together you shape its answer into one or two short phrases, such as 'may you be safe from ridicule' or 'may your work be respected', and check that the part agrees with the wording. At home you sit for about ten minutes a day, sense the part nearby and silently offer yourself those phrases on its behalf, noticing whether the critic softens, stays the same or objects.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose self-criticism is loud and familiar and who find that arguing with it or ignoring it has not helped. It may suit those who like structured meditation but want it tied to their own inner voices.
modalities.cautions: Not yet studied: turning toward a critical part can stir old shame or bring more hurt parts forward, so stop if feelings become intense and work with a licensed clinician trained in parts work, especially with a trauma history, dissociation or a current crisis. Wishing yourself well can at first bring grief or a sense of being unworthy, which is a reason to keep sessions short rather than push through.
modalities.tweet: Your inner critic might want something good for you underneath the shouting, like being safe or respected. The Critic's Real Wish is a new concept: ask it, turn the answer into a kind wish, and offer it to yourself, starting with a parts-work therapist.

modalities.name: One Part, Steadily Seen
modalities.tagline: Rest steady, wordless attention on one familiar part for a while.
modalities.whatItIs: One Part, Steadily Seen is an untested concept that brings the steady attention of concentration meditation into parts work. After settling the mind on the breath, you choose one part you already know, such as a worrier you feel as a tight jaw, and make its felt presence your single object for a quarter of an hour, without questioning it. Only familiar parts are used, nothing is meant to uncover forgotten events, and any images that appear are treated as inner experience, not evidence.
modalities.coreIdea: Parts work often moves quickly into conversation, but a part may show more of itself to attention that stays quiet and unhurried, the way a shy animal comes closer to someone sitting still. Concentration supplies that steadiness, so the part is witnessed for a long stretch rather than interviewed.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist trained in parts work who also teaches meditation guides the first sessions: about ten minutes of breath concentration, then 10 to 15 minutes resting attention on where and how one familiar part is felt in the body, returning to it gently whenever attention wanders. You do not ask questions or try to change the part, though you notice what shifts, such as warmth, loosening or a sense of its age. You finish by thanking the part and noting a few words about what you noticed, and after a few guided weeks you practice at home with regular check-ins.
modalities.whoItsFor: People in parts work who find the inner dialogue too busy or wordy and want a quieter way to get to know a part. It may suit meditators who already sit steadily and want that steadiness to serve inner work.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: long, steady attention on a part can bring up strong emotion or let more hurt parts surface, and concentrated sitting can bring fear or unusual sensations, so work with a licensed clinician trained in parts work and experienced with meditation-related difficulties, open your eyes and stop whenever you need to, and do not take it onto an intensive retreat. People with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should be screened by a clinician first, and it is not suited to a current crisis.
modalities.tweet: What if you got to know an inner part not by talking to it but by sitting with it, quietly and steadily, the way you might wait for a shy animal to come closer? One Part, Steadily Seen is a speculative practice, learned with a parts-work therapist.

modalities.name: Stepping Out to Watch
modalities.tagline: Move as one of your parts, then step aside and watch.
modalities.whatItIs: Stepping Out to Watch is a proposed group practice that brings the parts work of Internal Family Systems into dance movement therapy. You let a familiar part move you for a minute or two, with its own pace, posture and rhythm, then physically step out of that space to a witness line and look back at where it danced, with curiosity. Only parts you already know are used, it is never used to uncover forgotten events, and what comes up is treated as expression, not evidence about the past.
modalities.coreIdea: Parts work calls the moment you separate from a part 'unblending', and it can be hard to feel in words alone. Stepping out of a movement and turning to watch gives that separation a physical form, so the difference between being run by a part and seeing it may become something the body knows.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to ten people meet weekly for 75 minutes with a dance movement therapist trained in parts work, beginning with a warm-up to music. In turn, each person chooses a part, such as a hurried pleaser or a sulky protector, moves as it in the center of the room for one or two minutes, then steps out to a line of tape at the edge, watches the empty space while describing the part aloud, and finally moves again in whatever way feels like their own calm center. The group reflects back only what they saw, without interpreting the part.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it easier to express inner states through movement than through talk. It may suit those in parts work who want a livelier, more embodied way to practice stepping back from a part.
modalities.cautions: Untested: moving as a part can stir strong feelings or memories, so it belongs with a credentialed dance movement therapist who also has trauma training, and anyone can stop, sit out or just watch. Warm up first, keep the floor clear and non-slip, move within your own range of joints and balance, stop if you feel dizzy or unwell, and no touch is used.
modalities.tweet: Let a part of you dance for a minute, maybe the hurried people-pleaser, then step out of its spot and watch where it was. Stepping Out to Watch is an experimental group idea, led by a dance therapist, about being a part versus seeing it.

modalities.name: The Kind-Week Trial
modalities.tagline: Test whether being kind to yourself really makes you slack off.
modalities.whatItIs: The Kind-Week Trial is a proposed, untested experiment that brings the CBT habit of testing beliefs to loving-kindness meditation. Many people hold back from self-kindness because they expect it to make them lazy or sloppy, so you compare an ordinary week with a week of daily goodwill practice and record what actually happens to your work and mood.
modalities.coreIdea: A fear like 'if I go easy on myself, I'll stop trying' is a prediction, and CBT treats predictions as things to check. Running the comparison yourself, with simple records, is meant to give you your own evidence about whether goodwill and effort really pull against each other.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a CBT practitioner or a short structured course, you write down your prediction, such as 'I'll finish fewer tasks', and pick two or three simple measures, such as tasks completed, hours worked and an evening mood rating. In week one you live as usual and keep the records; in week two you add ten minutes each morning of goodwill phrases toward yourself, such as 'may I work steadily and kindly', and keep the same records. You then compare the two weeks with the practitioner, decide what the results suggest and, if you like, repeat the trial in another area of life.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who suspect that their harshness toward themselves is what keeps them productive and are curious to check. It may also suit those who like data and want a clear, structured reason to try a kindness practice.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea, and one week is a small sample, so treat the result as a hint rather than proof; wishing yourself well can at first stir grief or a sense of being unworthy, so keep sessions short. If harsh self-talk comes with severe low mood or thoughts of self-harm, see a mental health professional promptly rather than relying on an experiment.
modalities.tweet: Many of us avoid self-kindness because we expect it to make us lazy. The Kind-Week Trial, a new idea, tests that: one normal week, one week of ten-minute kindness practice, with your tasks and mood counted in both. Your own data, not a promise.

modalities.name: The Hindrance Flowchart
modalities.tagline: Name what is blocking your concentration, then try its planned response.
modalities.whatItIs: The Hindrance Flowchart is a speculative training method that brings CBT's step-by-step problem solving to concentration meditation. Buddhist teaching names five classic obstacles to concentration (craving, ill will, dullness, restlessness and worry, and doubt), and here each one gets a short written check and a matching, pre-planned step, so a frustrating sit becomes a problem you can work through.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT breaks a vague problem into named pieces with concrete next steps, and 'I just can't concentrate' is exactly that kind of vague problem. Identifying which obstacle is present, and answering it with one planned step instead of general effort, is meant to make concentration practice more learnable and less discouraging.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over six weekly sessions, a CBT practitioner who also teaches meditation helps you build a one-page chart: for each obstacle, a sign to look for, such as heavy eyelids for dullness, and one response to try, such as sitting up straighter and opening the eyes slightly, or counting breaths when restless. You sit for 15 to 25 minutes a day on the breath, use the chart when a sit stalls, and afterward note in a log which obstacle came up and whether the planned step helped. Each week you review the log together and revise the chart.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to develop deeper concentration but get discouraged by vague advice to just come back to the breath. It may suit those who like checklists and visible progress.
modalities.cautions: Untested: deeper concentration can bring strong body sensations, altered perception, fear or low mood, especially as practice lengthens, so build up gradually with a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties and do not move on to long retreats without one. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first, and this is a meditation skill, not a substitute for care for worry or depression.
modalities.tweet: Bad meditation sessions often feel like one vague failure. The Hindrance Flowchart, an experimental idea, names five classic obstacles, like dullness or restlessness, and gives each a planned response to try and log. Built slowly, with a teacher.

modalities.name: Whose Step Was It?
modalities.tagline: Partner dance mishaps as practice in sharing out blame fairly.
modalities.whatItIs: Whose Step Was It? is a proposed partner dance class that borrows a CBT exercise for people who blame themselves for everything. Partner dancing produces many small, harmless mishaps where responsibility really is shared, such as a missed turn or a tangle of arms, and after each one both partners estimate their own share before comparing notes.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT uses a 'responsibility pie' to show that most outcomes have many causes, because people prone to guilt tend to claim the whole pie. A dance figure gone wrong is a quick, low-stakes outcome with exactly two contributors, so dividing it fairly, over and over, is meant to make sharing responsibility feel normal.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over eight weekly 75-minute classes, a dance teacher who has trained with a CBT practitioner leads a warm-up and teaches simple partner figures to music, with partners rotating every few songs. Whenever a figure goes wrong, each partner quickly says what share out of ten they think was theirs, then hears the other's estimate and sometimes the teacher's view, before trying again. Between classes you draw one simple pie chart for an everyday mishap, such as a late delivery or a tense meeting, dividing it among everything that contributed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to assume that whatever goes wrong is their fault, and who would enjoy learning to dance. No dance experience is needed.
modalities.cautions: Untested: estimating blame can stir self-critical feelings, so keep it light, and if guilt or low mood is heavy or lasting, see a mental health professional. Warm up, dance on a clear, non-slip floor at your own level, stop if you feel pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness, check with a doctor first if you have heart, joint or balance problems, and agree on holds with each partner before dancing.
modalities.tweet: Partner dancing gives you lots of tiny, harmless mistakes that belong to two people. What if each one became practice in not taking all the blame? Whose Step Was It? is a new concept: dance, split each mishap fairly, then try the same in daily life.

modalities.name: Warmth Optional
modalities.tagline: Offer a wish, then do one kind act, whatever you feel.
modalities.whatItIs: Warmth Optional is a new, untested practice that joins loving-kindness meditation with ACT's focus on values and action. You offer a short wish to one person, notice whatever shows up, whether warmth, nothing or even irritation, and then do one small kind thing for them that day regardless.
modalities.coreIdea: Loving-kindness practice often aims to produce a warm feeling, and many people give up when it does not come. ACT treats caring as something you can choose to do even when the feeling is missing, so here the act counts whether or not the glow appears.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over a six-week course with a facilitator trained in ACT, and then on your own, you sit for about ten minutes each morning, bring one person to mind, silently offer a wish such as 'may your day go easily', and name what you feel without trying to change it. You then choose one small, concrete act of care for that person, such as a message, a coffee or holding back a sharp comment, and do it that day. In the evening you note whether you did it and what it was like, keeping no score of how warm you felt.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find that loving-kindness meditation leaves them feeling flat or fake, and who want their kindness to show in what they do. It may suit those who care about their relationships but feel numb or tired.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: noticing a lack of warmth toward someone can stir guilt or sadness, so keep sessions short and gentle, and choose kind acts that are safe and respect your own limits. Acting kindly is never a reason to stay close to someone who harms you, and lasting numbness or low mood is worth discussing with a mental health professional.
modalities.tweet: Loving-kindness meditation can feel fake when the warm feeling won't come. Warmth Optional is an untested idea: offer one person a wish, notice whatever you feel, then do one small kind thing for them anyway. The act counts, glow or no glow.

modalities.name: Shelter or Springboard
modalities.tagline: Check whether each concentration sit is a hiding place or a launch.
modalities.whatItIs: Shelter or Springboard is a speculative way of practicing concentration meditation with one of ACT's core questions built in. Deep calm can be a resource for your life or a place to hide from it, so each sit opens by naming what it is for and closes by checking whether you used the calm to move toward something you care about or away from something hard.
modalities.coreIdea: ACT sorts actions into moves toward what matters and moves away from discomfort, and meditation can be either. Asking that question at both ends of every sit is meant to keep the steadiness of concentration in service of a valued life rather than turning it into another way of avoiding it.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn the routine over a few sessions with a meditation teacher trained in ACT, then sit at home for about 25 minutes a day. For the first two minutes you write one line answering 'what is this sit for today?', then rest attention on the breath, gathering it back each time it strays, and in the final three minutes you ask honestly whether part of you was hiding from something, such as a hard conversation or a task. If so, you write down that thing, one small step toward it and when you will take it.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who love the calm of concentration and suspect they sometimes use it to put off things that matter. It may suit people interested in ACT who want a daily practice with values built in.
modalities.cautions: Untested: absorbed concentration can bring strong sensations, fear, or low mood after pleasant states, so build up gradually with a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties and avoid intensive retreats without one. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first, and severe depression or suicidal thoughts call for a qualified clinician rather than self-help.
modalities.tweet: Meditation can steady you for life, or quietly help you hide from it. Shelter or Springboard is a new concept: each concentration sit starts by naming what it is for and ends by asking honestly whether you were avoiding something you care about.

modalities.name: Three Dances, One Scarf
modalities.tagline: Hide it, shake it, or let it come: one feeling, three dances.
modalities.whatItIs: Three Dances, One Scarf is a proposed group dance session that turns ACT's ideas about struggling with feelings into something you can compare in your body. Each dancer ties a light scarf loosely to one wrist to stand for a feeling they wish would go away, such as nervousness or sadness, and dances the same song three ways: hiding the scarf, trying to shake it off, and letting it swing along while dancing toward something they value.
modalities.coreIdea: ACT holds that hiding from or fighting a hard feeling can cost more than the feeling itself, while making room for it frees you to move toward what matters. Dancing all three versions back to back is meant to let you feel that difference directly, in cramped arms, a tired shake or a looser, freer dance, rather than take it on trust.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 60-minute session led by a dance or movement facilitator trained in ACT, eight to twelve people warm up, name a feeling for the scarf and pick one word for what they want to move toward, such as play or connection. The same three-minute song plays three times: first you dance keeping the scarf out of sight, then trying to shake it off, and finally letting it come along while you dance toward your word, pausing after each round to notice your breath, your shoulders and your mood. The group ends seated in a circle, and each person names one moment in the coming week when the feeling could come along too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who understand acceptance in theory but struggle to feel it, and who enjoy moving to music. It may suit those who notice they spend a lot of energy hiding or fighting their feelings.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: naming a hard feeling can make it stronger for a while, so keep to everyday feelings rather than trauma, and see a mental health professional for anything severe. Warm up, keep the floor clear and non-slip, dance at your own level, stop if you feel pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness, check with a doctor first if you have heart, joint or balance problems, and keep scarves loose and easy to slip off.
modalities.tweet: Dance the same song three times with a scarf on your wrist standing for a feeling you dislike: hide it, shake it off, then let it swing along. Three Dances, One Scarf is an experimental group idea for feeling what struggling with a feeling costs. 🧣

modalities.name: Trick Swap Nights
modalities.tagline: A lively, unplanned evening of showing each other small tricks.
modalities.whatItIs: Trick Swap Nights is an untested idea for lively get-togethers where people teach each other small, hands-on tricks, such as a card shuffle, a paper fold, a coin roll or a two-finger whistle. There is no program and no host running things: people wander, show, fumble, laugh and swap, and the evening goes wherever it goes.
modalities.coreIdea: Loving-kindness meditation sends goodwill silently, in a set order, to people you picture; this goes the opposite way, toward a noisy room of real people handing each other something you can see and try. Nobody is asked to feel anything, and any connection comes from the plain, lively exchange.
modalities.whatYouDo: Anyone can start one by inviting a mix of friends and acquaintances to a kitchen, garden or community room and asking each to bring one small trick they can show in a couple of minutes, with props such as cards, string or paper. Once people arrive there is no running order: you drift between little clusters, ask someone to show you their trick, show yours when asked, and swap partners whenever you like. It ends when people drift home, often planning to show someone else.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find small talk hard but feel at ease when their hands have something to do. It may also suit anyone who wants a livelier, lower-pressure way to meet new people.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: being shown up or teased can sting, so keep the mood generous, and anyone can watch instead of performing. Keep props safe (no fire, blades or anything thrown hard), and if social situations bring intense fear or panic, talk to a doctor or therapist rather than pushing through alone.
modalities.tweet: Bring one small trick you can teach in two minutes (a card shuffle, a paper fold, a two-finger whistle) and swap with whoever is nearby. Trick Swap Nights is a new idea for loud, unplanned evenings where your hands get the conversation started.

modalities.name: Quiet Company Hikes
modalities.tagline: A long, steady hike with friends, in shared silence.
modalities.whatItIs: Quiet Company Hikes is a speculative way of hiking in which two to five companions walk a long route together in near silence, with no plan beyond the route and a turnaround time. Nothing is wished, discussed or worked on: the company is simply there, step for step, in the same weather and the same landscape.
modalities.coreIdea: Loving-kindness meditation fills the mind with words of goodwill for people who are not there; this goes the other way, to real people who are there and no words at all. Company that asks for nothing, not even kind thoughts, plus steady effort through open country, is meant to let everything be just as it is.
modalities.whatYouDo: You agree on a route of three to five hours at a steady, hard but sustainable effort, a turnaround time and a few safety signals, then walk the first ten minutes chatting and warming up before settling into silence. Along the way you keep to the group's pace and stop together for water and food without needing to talk, using speech only for route and safety. At the end you can talk as much or as little as you like, or simply go home.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are tired of talking, or who feel closest to friends when nothing needs to be said. It may suit those who love hiking but find group walks too chatty.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: plan the route, check the weather, carry water, food, layers and a map or charged phone, tell someone where you are going, and agree that anyone can break the silence at any moment for safety or comfort. The effort is real, so check with a doctor first if you have heart, lung or joint problems, warm up, and stop and speak up at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: An idea for friends who love hills: walk three to five hours together in shared silence. Quiet Company Hikes keep speech for route and safety only, so the company, the effort and the landscape can be enough. Plan well, and anyone may break the silence.

modalities.name: What You Are Wearing
modalities.tagline: Feel your clothes on your skin, plainly, from feet to collar.
modalities.whatItIs: What You Are Wearing is a new, untested sensory practice in which you spend a few quiet minutes feeling exactly what your clothes are doing on your skin: the weight of a jumper, the edge of a sock, the band of a waistline, the slight drag of a sleeve. You add nothing and change nothing: the practice is only to notice what is already touching you all day.
modalities.coreIdea: Loving-kindness meditation wraps people in imagined warmth and chosen words; this goes the other way, to what actually wraps you, plain fabric on plain skin, with no picture, no wish and nobody else in mind. Sensations we stop noticing within minutes of dressing make a ready, private place for attention to land.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a day, alone, you sit or stand still for five to ten minutes and move attention through your clothes from the feet upward: socks or shoes, the cloth over the legs, the waistband, the fabric over the back and chest, then the collar and sleeves. At each place you notice pressure, texture, warmth or coolness and any small movement with the breath, then move on, letting whatever you feel stay as it is. If a garment is uncomfortable you notice that too, and afterward you are free to change it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a short, private sensory practice they can do anywhere without anyone noticing. It may suit those who find kindness phrases or imagery hard and prefer something entirely plain.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea and generally low risk, though close attention to the body can sometimes bring up anxiety, discomfort or memories, so keep it short and stop if it does. People with a trauma history, or who feel distress about their body, may find it gentler with a trained teacher or therapist, and it is not a stand-alone treatment for anxiety or any other condition.
modalities.tweet: Right now your clothes are pressing, brushing and warming you in a dozen places you stopped noticing. What You Are Wearing is a new idea: five quiet minutes feeling them from socks to collar, adding nothing and changing nothing.

modalities.name: Tuesday Blues Jam
modalities.tagline: Sing the week's small troubles as blues, with a group answering back.
modalities.whatItIs: Tuesday Blues Jam is a proposed, loose weekly gathering where people take turns singing a short blues verse about something that actually went wrong, from a broken boiler to a lonely weekend, while the room claps, sways and sings an answering line. No one has to sing well, and nothing has to be turned into a positive.
modalities.coreIdea: Loving-kindness meditation answers hard feelings alone, in silence, with gentle wishes; this goes the other way, letting the real grumbles of a life be heard out loud, in company, exactly as they are. The blues has long turned troubles into something shared and even fun, and that sharing, not a change of heart, is the point.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to fifteen people meet for about 90 minutes in a home, cafe or community room, where a volunteer musician keeps a simple, slow blues going on guitar or keyboard. Whoever wants a turn sings or speaks a verse of a few lines about their week, or about something older they already remember and choose to share, and the group answers with a repeated line such as 'yes, we hear you', clapping, stomping and swaying as they like. Turns are short and voluntary, and the evening ends with a couple of rowdy group verses.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find relentlessly positive self-help tiring and would rather have their troubles heard than talked away. It may suit those who like music and company but have no musical training.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: dwelling on troubles can deepen a low mood for some people, so keep verses light, skip turns freely, notice how you feel afterward and talk to a doctor or therapist if low mood lingers. Verses are about your own life, never about people in the room, it is no place to work through trauma, and the volume stays moderate to protect everyone's hearing.
modalities.tweet: Once a week, take a turn singing a short blues verse about what actually went wrong (the boiler, the bus, the lonely weekend) while the room claps and sings back. Tuesday Blues Jam is a new concept: troubles heard, not talked away. No talent needed.

modalities.name: Float the Room
modalities.tagline: At a lively gathering, drift through many conversations without settling.
modalities.whatItIs: Float the Room is an untested idea for busy parties and gatherings in which you deliberately drift between many conversations, staying a few minutes in each, rather than settling into one corner with one person. It is pure talk and listening, lively and loose, with no plan for whom you meet.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana meditation gathers attention onto one object for a long time, alone and in silence; this goes the other way, spreading attention lightly across a whole noisy room of people. Many short, real contacts in one evening are meant to make a crowd feel like a set of small, friendly openings rather than one big wall.
modalities.whatYouDo: At a party, mixer, festival tent or community event, you give yourself a loose aim of joining five or six different conversations over an hour or two. You walk up to a group with an easy opener, such as 'mind if I join you?' or a comment on the food or music, listen and chip in for a few minutes, then leave warmly ('lovely to meet you, I'm off to grab a drink') and drift to the next. Nothing is recorded or rated, and you stop whenever you have had enough.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to get stuck with one person at gatherings, or who freeze at the thought of joining a group. It may suit those who enjoy lively company and want to widen their circle a little.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: walking up to strangers can feel uncomfortable, so start with easier events or with a friend, leave any group that feels unwelcoming, and favor safe, public settings. If social situations bring intense fear, panic or avoidance, this may be social anxiety, which is treatable, so talk to a doctor or therapist rather than pushing through alone.
modalities.tweet: At your next party, try not to spend the whole night in one conversation. Float the Room is a speculative practice: join five or six groups for a few minutes each, leave warmly, drift on. Lots of small, real hellos instead of one long corner.

modalities.name: The Long Way to Lunch
modalities.tagline: A good long hike with friends, and lunch somewhere lovely.
modalities.whatItIs: The Long Way to Lunch is a proposed way of hiking with a few friends that is built around plain outward pleasures: the climb, the view, the sun or wind on your face and a picnic at the best spot you can find. There is no route plan beyond a rough, known loop and a turnaround time, no technique and nothing to achieve.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana practice turns away from the pleasures of the senses and finds joy within, through years of training; this goes the other way, letting the outside world supply the pleasure, shared with friends, with no skill required. Hunger, effort and a good view are allowed to be enough.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two to six friends pick a hilly loop of a few hours, pack a picnic and set off at a steady, hard but chatty pace after an easy first ten minutes. Along the way anyone can call a stop for a view, a stream or a patch of sun, and you keep an eye out for the best lunch spot, settling there as long as you like to eat slowly and look around. The walk home follows whatever known, safe path feels good.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find meditation and self-improvement too effortful and want something that simply feels good. It may suit friends who want a regular, unhurried reason to be outdoors together.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: plan the route, check the weather, carry water, layers and a map or charged phone, tell someone where you are going, and take all food waste home. The climbing is real effort, so check with a doctor first if you have heart, lung or joint problems, warm up on the flat, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: What if a hike's only goal was a great lunch spot? The Long Way to Lunch is a new idea: a few friends, a hilly loop, a stop for every good view, and a slow picnic wherever it looks best. Plan the route, check the weather, enjoy.

modalities.name: Hands in the Jar
modalities.tagline: Sink your hands into dry rice, lentils or sand, and feel.
modalities.whatItIs: Hands in the Jar is a speculative sensory practice in which you sink your hands slowly into a few bowls of plain material, such as dry rice, lentils, sand or cool water, and feel what happens. You keep your eyes open or closed, move or rest the fingers as you like, and let each texture be whatever it is.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana meditation lets the senses fade as attention withdraws into rare inner states that take years and a teacher to reach; this goes the other way, into coarse, unmistakable sensation that anyone can feel within seconds. The materials are vivid and the hands are sensitive, so nothing needs to be mastered or attained.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone at a table, you set out three or four bowls, each with a different material, and spend about three minutes with each, letting your hands sink in, spread, close and rest while you feel weight, grain, temperature and the way the material moves. Between bowls you rest your hands on the table for a few breaths and notice what lingers. A session takes 15 to 20 minutes, and afterward the materials go back into their jars for next time.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find sitting meditation too subtle or effortful and want something tangible and simple. It may suit anyone who settles more easily when their hands are busy.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea and generally low risk: keep small materials away from young children and pets, skip them if you have cuts or a skin condition on your hands, and wash your hands afterward. Close attention to sensation can occasionally bring up anxiety or memories, so stop if it does, and it is not a stand-alone treatment for anxiety or any other condition.
modalities.tweet: A bowl of dry rice, one of lentils, one of cool water, and your hands sinking slowly into each. Hands in the Jar is an untested idea for a plain, tangible sensory pause: no skill, no goal, just texture, weight and temperature.

modalities.name: Family Songbook Nights
modalities.tagline: Relatives of every age swap and sing the songs of their youth.
modalities.whatItIs: Family Songbook Nights is a new, untested idea for relatives, or close friends who feel like family, to meet now and then and teach each other songs from different times in their lives, from a grandparent's dance hall tune to a teenager's current favorite. Everyone sings, claps or plays along, and each song goes into a shared, handwritten songbook with a line about who brought it.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana is practiced alone, in silence, on one unchanging object; this goes the other way, to many voices, many songs and the shared history of the people singing them. Songs carry a family's past, and passing them between generations is meant to let people hear a little more of each other's lives.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every month or two a household or extended family gathers for an evening, often around a meal, and three or four people each bring one song from their own life, play a recording or sing it, say a sentence about where it comes from and teach the chorus. The others sing along, clap, add harmonies or dance in the kitchen, and someone writes the song and its story into the songbook. There is no running order and no rehearsal, and anyone can simply listen.
modalities.whoItsFor: Families and close groups of friends who want something warmer than conversation alone to bring the generations together. It may suit relatives who live close by but rarely do anything together.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: a song tied to someone who has died or moved away can bring grief, and family gatherings are not safe or comfortable for everyone, so choose relatives you feel at ease with and let anyone pass. Share only memories you already have and want to tell, keep the volume moderate, and if a song leaves feelings that stay heavy, talk to someone you trust or a therapist.
modalities.tweet: Grandma's dance hall tune, Dad's road trip song, your niece's latest favorite: Family Songbook Nights is a new idea for teaching each other the songs of your lives, singing them together, and writing each one down with a line about who brought it.

modalities.name: Funniest Thing This Week
modalities.tagline: Sit around a table and trade this week's funny moments.
modalities.whatItIs: Funniest Thing This Week is a proposed, almost structureless get-together where friends sit around a table, with no music and no plan, and trade the small funny things that happened to them lately: a misheard announcement, a cat's latest crime, a typo that went to the whole office. It is all talk and laughter, and nobody has to perform.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance brings people together through moving bodies, music and rhythm; this pushes socializing the other way, to people sitting still with nothing but words and attention, where laughing at each other's stories does the connecting. Keeping to recent, everyday moments keeps it light and open to everyone, not only natural storytellers.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every couple of weeks, five to twelve people gather in a kitchen, pub corner or living room for an evening, with drinks and snacks but no music on. Someone starts with the funniest small thing from their week, others jump in with their own or with questions, and the talk goes wherever it goes, with no turns and no scoring. Teasing stays affectionate, and the stories are about everyday moments, not about mocking anyone, present or absent.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want lighter, easier company and would rather laugh with friends than discuss serious topics. It may suit those who are not into dancing, sport or loud venues but enjoy a lively table.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea and generally low risk: humor that targets someone can hurt, so keep it kind, and nobody has to share. If social situations bring intense fear, or low mood keeps you away from people, talk to a doctor or therapist rather than pushing through alone.
modalities.tweet: No music, no plan, no performing: just friends around a table trading the week's small funny moments. That is the whole of Funniest Thing This Week, an untested idea for easier, lighter company.

modalities.name: Nose-First Wandering
modalities.tagline: A slow, solitary walk where scent decides which way you go.
modalities.whatItIs: Nose-First Wandering is an experimental way of taking a slow walk alone in a park, wood or field, letting smell decide where you go next: toward wet earth, cut grass, pine resin, a hedge in flower or the sea. You walk unhurriedly, stop often, breathe in and drift on, with no route, no rhythm and nothing to show for it.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance is rhythmic, expressive movement, often to music and in company; this pushes the walk the other way, toward the quietest, least showy sense and a body that moves only as slowly as it likes, alone. Following a scent gives attention a soft, receptive thread instead of a beat to keep.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose a safe, familiar green space, set aside 30 to 60 minutes with your phone silenced, and walk slowly, pausing whenever a smell catches you to breathe it in for a few breaths, then turning toward whatever you smell next. You may crouch near soil or bark, but you smell only, without picking, touching or tasting unfamiliar plants. You end by sitting for a few minutes before heading home.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want an outdoor walk that is gentle, calming and completely without goals. It may suit those who feel overloaded by sights and screens and want to give a quieter sense the lead.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: stay on paths in places you know so the wandering does not get you lost, check the weather, tell someone where you are, and watch for traffic, uneven ground and ticks. People with allergies, asthma or hay fever should take care in pollen season, and you should never eat or rub unfamiliar plants.
modalities.tweet: Let your nose choose the route. Nose-First Wandering is a speculative slow walk alone through a park or wood, turning toward wet earth, cut grass or pine and pausing to breathe it in. Stay on paths you know, and smell but don't pick.

modalities.name: Under the Weight
modalities.tagline: Lie still under a weighted blanket and feel the pressure settle.
modalities.whatItIs: Under the Weight is a speculative sensory practice in which you lie alone and completely still under a weighted blanket for about 20 minutes, feeling the even pressure across your body and how it rises and falls with each breath. The steps are simple and the same each time, and nothing is meant to happen except feeling it.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance carries the body through space, against gravity, to music and with other people; this goes the other way, letting weight press a still body down, alone and in silence. Steady, even pressure is a strong, plain sensation that is easy to keep returning to.
modalities.whatYouDo: You lie on your back on a bed or mat in a quiet room and draw the blanket up to your chest, leaving your head, neck and arms free. For 20 minutes you move attention slowly from the feet upward, feeling where the weight presses, where it is lighter and how it shifts with the breath, then let attention rest on the whole spread of pressure. You finish by folding the blanket back, lying for a minute without it and noticing the difference.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like deep pressure and find it settling, and who want a simple, solitary way to rest attention in the body. It may suit those who find it hard to lie still without something to anchor them.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: weighted blankets are not suitable for young children, for people with breathing, circulation, heart or mobility problems, or for anyone who cannot easily push one off, so ask a doctor if unsure. Choose one that you can lift and move easily (makers often suggest about a tenth of body weight), keep it off the face and neck, stop if you feel trapped, overheated or anxious, and do not rely on it for sleep or anxiety problems.
modalities.tweet: Twenty minutes, alone, lying still under a weighted blanket, feeling where it presses and how it rises with each breath. Under the Weight is an untested idea for a quiet sensory rest. Not for young children or anyone with breathing or circulation problems.

modalities.name: Letters to a Song
modalities.tagline: Write a letter to a song that has stayed with you.
modalities.whatItIs: Letters to a Song is a proposed small-group writing practice in which you sit with a song that has accompanied part of your life, listen to it once, and write it a letter as if it were an old friend: where you first heard it, what it got you through, what you hear in it now. Reading aloud is optional, and the rest of the group simply listens.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance answers music with the body, in the moment; this pushes music the other way, toward stillness, words and reflection, answering a song slowly from a chair. Writing to a song, rather than about it, is meant to draw out the personal meaning it carries in a gentle, playful form.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to eight people meet monthly for about 90 minutes with a facilitator, such as a writing group leader or a music therapist, and each brings one song. Each song is played once at a moderate volume, then everyone writes for about 15 minutes to their own song, starting 'Dear song', and those who want to read their letters aloud while the others listen, answering only with thanks. The group ends by playing a few seconds of each song again.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who love music and like to write, or who find it easier to say personal things to a song than to a person. No musical knowledge or writing skill is needed.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: songs tied to hard times can bring back strong feelings, and for people prone to rumination sad music can deepen a low mood, so choose a song you can sit with, share only what you already remember and wish to tell, and stop if it becomes heavy. It is not a substitute for therapy, and anyone with lasting low mood should talk to a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: Dear song, you got me through my first winter away from home... Letters to a Song is a new concept: in a small group, play a song that has stayed with you, write it a letter as if to an old friend, and read it aloud only if you want to. ✉️
